The number of DEGs (C100) is documented in Figure 4c and Figure 4—figure supplement 1b-c. GSEA analysis (C101-C102) showing pathway overlap is presented in Figure 4d and Figure 4—figure supplement 1f-h. Minimal UV-associated changes (C99) are shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a-b.

results.result: RNASeq analysis of MN+ versus MN- cells after Mps1i treatment revealed minimal transcriptional differences, with samples clustering by replicate rather than MN status and only two genes (EGR1 and TNFAIP3) upregulated >1.5-fold, both also upregulated in bulk Mps1i analysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C31, C104-C108 describe the lack of MN-specific transcriptional response. Clustering by replicate (C105) is shown in Figure 5b. Few DEGs (C106) are documented in Figure 5c and Figure 5—figure supplement 1i. The two upregulated genes (C107) are shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1cj. Nuclear atypia analysis (C104) is in Figure 5—figure supplement 1a. The conclusion (C108) is well-supported by the data.

results.result: RNASeq analysis of intact versus ruptured MN+ cells identified 14 DEGs with >1.5-fold change, but GSEA showed almost complete overlap with bulk Mps1i pathways. Immunofluorescence validation showed no increase in EGR1 and only a small shift in ATF3 in ruptured MN cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C117 describe the minimal unique transcriptional effects of MN rupture. Clustering by condition (C109) is shown in Figure 5e. The 14 DEGs (C110-C111) are documented in Figure 5f and Figure 5—figure supplement 1k-l. GSEA overlap (C112) is shown in Figure 5g and Figure 5—figure supplement 1m-n. Immunofluorescence validation (C115-C116) is presented in Figure 6b-c. The conclusion (C117) is well-supported.

results.result: DNA-FISH analysis revealed that aneuploidy frequency was consistently higher in MN+ versus MN- cells and higher in ruptured versus intact MN+ cells for 2/3 chromosomes tested, suggesting that transcriptional changes in micronucleated cells correlate with slightly increased aneuploidy rather than MN formation or rupture per se.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C118-C121 describe the relationship between MN status and aneuploidy. Aneuploidy frequency differences (C118-C119) are shown in Figure 6e. The conclusion that micronucleated cells have slightly higher aneuploidy (C120) and that MN formation/rupture don't cause specific transcriptional changes (C121) is well-supported by the combined RNASeq and DNA-FISH data. This provides a mechanistic explanation for the observed transcriptional patterns.

results.result: In RPE1 cells, Mps1i treatment for 24 hours increased MN frequency from 3% to ~50%, with most MN+ nuclei having one MN containing a single chromosome. Mps1i also increased misshapen nuclei and chromatin bridges to lower levels than MN, with only misshapen nuclei slightly enriched in the MN+ population.
results.evaluation: Claims C34, C37-C42 describe the effects of Mps1i treatment on RPE1 cells. The increase in MN frequency (C37) is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b. The distribution of MN per nucleus (C40) and chromosome content (C41) are documented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1d-e. The lower frequency of other nuclear abnormalities (C38-C39) is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b-c. The conclusion (C42) is well-supported.

results.result: MN-nucleus assignment by proximity was accurate 97% of the time, with MN being on average 3.3 times closer to the nearest nucleus than the second nearest, suggesting robust assignment even at high cell densities where 10% of nuclei had borders <6 µm apart.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C52 describe the accuracy of proximity-based MN-nucleus assignment. The 97% accuracy (C49) is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2d-e. The 3.3-fold distance difference (C50) is documented in Figure 1—figure supplement 2g. The 10% of nuclei with borders <6 µm apart (C51) is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2h. The inference about robustness at high density (C52) is reasonable given the data.

results.result: VCS MN performed substantially worse on ×40 confocal images of DAPI-labeled RPE1 cells compared to the training set, with MN masks failing to cover most of the MN area.
results.evaluation: Claim C71 describes the poor performance of VCS MN on higher resolution confocal images. This is documented in Figure 2a with quantified recall and mIoU values. This observation motivated the development of MNFinder for fixed cell analysis.

results.result: The study demonstrates that MNFinder robustly segments MN across multiple cell types and imaging conditions, VCS MN rapidly identifies micronucleated cells and can be combined with photoconversion for live cell isolation, and visual cell sorting is suitable for bulk genomic analyses.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C124, C138 are summary statements about the overall capabilities of the developed methods. These are well-supported by the comprehensive performance data presented throughout the manuscript for both VCS MN and MNFinder, and the successful validation of visual cell sorting for transcriptome analysis.

results.result: Visual cell sorting has several advantages over existing methods: it works on any adherent cell line, overcomes limitations of lamin B2 overexpression and chromosome-specific missegregation systems, is highly scalable, captures whole live cells, and can be performed on attached cells using standard microscopy equipment.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C134 describe advantages of visual cell sorting over existing methods. These are well-reasoned comparisons supported by citations to prior literature (C126-C128, C129-C131, C133-C134) and logical inferences from the demonstrated capabilities of the method. The claims are appropriately framed as advantages rather than direct experimental comparisons.

results.result: Visual cell sorting and the MN segmentation modules have limitations: only ~200,000 cells can be analyzed per experiment due to Dendra2 decay and ongoing rupture, the method requires introduction of fluorescent proteins, and performance may vary with divergent nuclear morphologies.
results.evaluation: Claims C135-C137 describe limitations of the methods. These are honest assessments based on the experimental design (C135-C136) and observed performance variations (C137). The throughput limitation (C135) is a reasonable inference from the Dendra2 stability data and experimental timeline. The requirement for fluorescent proteins (C136) is inherent to the method design.

results.result: Comparison with previous studies showed large overlap in upregulated pathways but globally lower gene expression changes, which could reflect exclusion of highly lobulated nuclei and suggests nuclear atypia may contribute significantly to aneuploidy signaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C139-C141 compare the current results to previous studies and speculate about the role of nuclear atypia. While the pathway overlap (C139) is well-documented in Figure 4d and Figure 4—figure supplement 1f-h, the speculation about nuclear atypia (C140-C141) is not directly tested. The authors acknowledge this could also reflect technical variation in sequencing protocols. Additional experiments would be needed to definitively test this hypothesis.

results.result: The authors argue that cGAS bound to ruptured MN is incapable of activating STING based on prior literature, and expect that analysis in cGAS/STING-active cell lines would yield similar results to RPE1 cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C142-C144 address the potential limitation of using RPE1 cells with reduced cGAS expression. While the citations to prior literature (C142-C143) support the argument that cGAS recruitment to MN doesn't activate STING in the first cell cycle, the prediction that other cell lines would show similar results (C144) is speculative and not directly tested. This represents a reasonable hypothesis but requires experimental validation.

results.result: Visual cell sorting is proposed as a flexible platform for future applications including optical pooled screening, chromosome-specific MN analysis, disease behavior studies, and in vivo assays, enabling large-scale analyses of post-mitotic changes caused by micronucleation.
results.evaluation: Claims C145-C151 describe proposed future applications of visual cell sorting. These are reasonable extensions of the demonstrated capabilities (C148-C149) and well-reasoned proposals for future work (C146-C147, C150) supported by appropriate citations. The claims are appropriately framed as potential applications rather than demonstrated results. The summary statement (C151) accurately reflects the potential impact of the methods.

results.result: The manuscript provides extensive background on MN biology, including their role in genome instability, cancer, aging, and disease, the challenges of automated MN detection, and the use of Mps1 inhibition to induce MN formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4, C9-C27, C32-C33, C35-C36, C46, C62 provide background knowledge about MN biology and prior methods. These are well-supported by citations to prior literature and represent accurate summaries of established knowledge in the field. They provide appropriate context for the current work.

results.result: Deep Retina nucleus segmenter frequently missed highly lobulated nuclei, resulting in an image set with higher mean nuclear solidity than bulk Mps1i-treated cells.
results.evaluation: Claim C47 describes a limitation of the Deep Retina segmenter used for nucleus detection. This is documented in Figure 1—figure supplement 2b with quantified solidity measurements. This observation is important for interpreting the downstream analyses, particularly the RNASeq results.

results.result: VCS MN is a rapid neural network-based classifier that identifies micronucleated cells and their rupture status from low-resolution images. The tool achieved recall of 70% for MN and 65% for MN+ nuclei, with PPV of 89% and 93% respectively in RPE1 cells, and similar performance in U2OS cells.
results.evaluation: All reviewers acknowledged VCS MN as a valuable tool. Reviewer 1 stated the tools are 'powerful new tools' with 'rigorous and convincing' benchmarking. Reviewer 2 noted 'developing highly specialized tools...is likely valuable to the community.' Reviewer 3 confirmed 'the authors develop a method that allows for automating measurements and analysis of micronuclei' which 'has been something that the field has been missing.' No concerns were raised about VCS MN performance metrics.

results.result: MNFinder is a robust segmentation pipeline using ensemble neural networks that accurately segments micronuclei across multiple cell lines and imaging conditions. It achieved recall of 74-79% with mIoU values of 74-79%, outperforming existing tools in specificity while maintaining similar sensitivity.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirmed MNFinder's performance. Reviewer 1 stated 'the analysis of the new tools and their benchmarking is rigorous and convincing.' Reviewer 3 noted the software 'outperforms available tools for MN segmentation by providing mIoU' and acknowledged it as filling a gap since 'there are no robust MN classifiers with a clear quantification of their efficiency across cell lines.' The high mIoU metric was specifically recognized as important for quantifying MN characteristics.

results.result: VCS MN classifies MN rupture status using a Dendra2 fluorescence intensity threshold of 0.16, correctly classifying approximately 90% of MN and identifying 60% of rupture- nuclei and 70% of rupture+ nuclei with PPV near 75%.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not raise concerns about the rupture classification method. Reviewer 1 noted that 'applications and remaining limitations are well explained,' implicitly accepting the rupture detection capabilities. Reviewer 3 acknowledged the method 'to identify cells with micronuclei in real-time, mark them using photoconversion, and then isolate them via cell sorting' without questioning the rupture classification component.

results.result: Visual cell sorting combined with VCS MN and photoconversion enables isolation of live cells with none, intact, or ruptured MN with 95% sorting efficiency. The method achieved strong enrichment for correct cell types, with MN+ populations showing nearly 7-fold enrichment compared to starting populations.
results.evaluation: Reviewers strongly endorsed the visual cell sorting approach. Reviewer 2 stated 'combining automated analysis, single-cell labeling, and cell sorting is an exciting approach to enrich for phenotypes of interest, which the authors demonstrate here.' Reviewer 3 noted 'the authors develop a method to identify cells with micronuclei in real-time...which could change the way we isolate and study MN-containing cells, and the scale at which we do it' and called it 'very powerful as it can allow for the separation of a heterogenous population.'

results.result: Visual cell sorting successfully recapitulated established aneuploidy signatures in Mps1i-treated RPE1 cells, identifying 2200 DEGs with substantial overlap in inflammation, EMT, and p53 pathways compared to previous studies, validating the method for bulk transcriptomic analysis.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted the validation of visual cell sorting for transcriptomic analysis. Reviewer 1 noted the work is 'rigorous and convincing.' Reviewer 3 acknowledged 'the authors use this method to look at the transcriptome' and that it is 'very powerful' for population analysis. The successful recapitulation of known aneuploidy signatures was not questioned by any reviewer.

results.result: Neither micronucleation nor rupture triggers a strong unique transcriptional response in the first cell cycle after chromosome missegregation in RPE1 cells. RNASeq of MN+ vs MN- cells showed minimal differential gene expression, with only two genes (EGR1 and TNFAIP3) upregulated >1.5-fold.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 expressed significant concern about this finding, stating 'there is in general large variance between replicates in experiments looking at cells with ruptured versus intact micronuclei. This limits our ability to assess if lack of changes are due to truly not having changes between these populations or experimental limitations.' They concluded 'more transcriptomic analysis will be necessary to fully understand the downstream consequences of MN rupture,' indicating the evidence is insufficient to definitively support the claim of no transcriptional response.

results.result: MN rupture has minimal unique effects on transcription in the first interphase after chromosome missegregation. RNASeq of intact vs ruptured MN+ cells identified 14 DEGs with >1.5-fold changes, but pathway analysis showed almost complete overlap with bulk Mps1i populations, and validation showed no increase in EGR1 and only small shifts in ATF3.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 specifically highlighted this as a weakness: 'The major weakness of this paper is the transcriptomic analysis of MN. There is in general large variance between replicates in experiments looking at cells with ruptured versus intact micronuclei.' They noted this 'limits our ability to assess if lack of changes are due to truly not having changes between these populations or experimental limitations,' directly questioning whether the conclusion of minimal transcriptional effects is valid or an artifact of experimental limitations.

results.result: Transcriptional changes in micronucleated cells correlate with small increases in aneuploidy rather than micronucleation itself. Aneuploidy frequency was consistently higher for MN+ compared to MN- cells and higher for ruptured compared to intact MN+ cells for 2/3 chromosomes tested.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted this finding without raising concerns. Reviewer 2 summarized the work as showing 'they do not observe a transcriptomic signature specific to MN but find changes that correlate with aneuploidy status,' directly affirming this result. Reviewer 3 noted 'the authors find that RPE-1 cells with MN have similar transcriptomic changes as aneuploid cells,' also supporting this interpretation.

results.result: VCS MN and MNFinder precision vary across cell types and widely divergent nuclear morphologies from the training set could impair performance.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly raised this concern: 'Although the classifier outperforms available tools for MN segmentation by providing mIoU, it's not yet at a point where it can be reliably applied to functional genomics assays where we expect a range of phenotypic penetrance in most cell lines (e.g., misshapen, multinucleated, and lagging DNA in addition to micronucleated cells).' They noted 'whether the classifier can rigorously assign MN-presenting cells amidst drastic nuclear aberrancies following a spindle checkpoint loss needs to be tested in the future,' confirming this limitation.

results.result: Visual cell sorting offers multiple advantages over existing methods: it works on any adherent cell line, overcomes limitations of lamin B2 overexpression and chromosome-specific systems, is highly scalable, captures whole live cells, permits time-resolved analyses, and can be adapted to any wide-field microscope.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirmed these advantages. Reviewer 1 stated 'applications and remaining limitations are well explained in the paper.' Reviewer 2 noted 'combining automated analysis, single-cell labeling, and cell sorting is an exciting approach' and that 'developing highly specialized tools...is likely valuable to the community.' Reviewer 3 emphasized the method 'could change the way we isolate and study MN-containing cells, and the scale at which we do it,' supporting the claimed advantages.

results.result: Visual cell sorting has limitations: only about 200,000 live cells can be analyzed per experiment due to Dendra2 signal decay and ongoing MN rupture, and it requires introduction of photoconvertible and fluorescent proteins.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly noted that 'applications and remaining limitations are well explained in the paper,' indicating acceptance of the stated limitations. No reviewer challenged these specific limitations, and they are consistent with the technical requirements of the photoconversion approach that reviewers endorsed.

results.result: A globally lower change in gene expression levels was observed compared to previous studies, which could reflect exclusion of cells with highly lobulated nuclei from the analysis, suggesting nuclear atypia may be a significant contributor to aneuploidy signaling changes.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge this interpretation. Reviewer 3's concern about variance in the rupture experiments does not extend to questioning this observation about nuclear atypia. The speculation is presented as a potential explanation for observed differences and is consistent with the methodological approach of excluding highly lobulated nuclei, which reviewers accepted as part of the study design.

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluations support VCS MN's performance and capabilities (C5, C28, C43-C66). OpenEval provides detailed technical validation citing specific figures, while peer reviewers emphasize the tool's value to the community with descriptors like 'powerful' and 'rigorous and convincing.' Both agree the method is well-validated.

Both evaluations support MNFinder's architecture and performance (C6, C29, C72-C88). OpenEval details technical metrics and figure references, while peer reviewers highlight that it 'outperforms available tools' and fills a gap in the field. Both agree on the method's strong performance and benchmarking.

Both evaluations support the rupture classification method (C67-C70). OpenEval provides detailed validation with specific accuracy metrics and figure references. Peer reviewers implicitly accept the rupture detection capabilities without raising concerns, noting that 'applications and remaining limitations are well explained.'

Both evaluations strongly support visual cell sorting validation (C89-C97, C124). OpenEval details specific enrichment metrics and figure references. Peer reviewers enthusiastically endorse the approach as 'exciting' and 'very powerful,' noting it 'could change the way we isolate and study MN-containing cells.'

Both evaluations support the transcriptomic validation of visual cell sorting (C30, C98-C103, C138-C139). OpenEval details PCA clustering, DEG counts, and GSEA results with figure references. Peer reviewers accept the method as 'rigorous and convincing' and 'very powerful' for population analysis, including recapitulation of aneuploidy signatures.

Significant disagreement on lack of MN-specific transcriptional response (C7, C31, C104-C108, C121). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED with detailed figure references. Peer Reviewer 3 rates as UNCERTAIN, expressing concern about 'large variance between replicates' that 'limits our ability to assess if lack of changes are due to truly not having changes between these populations or experimental limitations.'

Significant disagreement on minimal transcriptional effects of MN rupture (C109-C117). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED citing 14 DEGs and validation data. Peer Reviewer 3 rates as UNCERTAIN, highlighting this as 'the major weakness of this paper' due to 'large variance between replicates,' questioning whether the minimal changes reflect biology or experimental limitations.

Both evaluations support the relationship between MN status and aneuploidy (C8, C118-C120). OpenEval details frequency differences and mechanistic explanations with figure references. Peer reviewers explicitly affirm this finding, with Reviewer 2 noting 'they do not observe a transcriptomic signature specific to MN but find changes that correlate with aneuploidy status.'

Both evaluations support the advantages of visual cell sorting over existing methods (C125-C134, C145). OpenEval notes these are well-reasoned comparisons supported by citations. Peer reviewers affirm the advantages, describing the approach as 'exciting' and noting it 'could change the way we isolate and study MN-containing cells, and the scale at which we do it.'

Both evaluations support the stated limitations regarding throughput and fluorescent protein requirements (C135-C136). OpenEval describes these as honest assessments based on experimental design. Peer Reviewer 1 explicitly notes 'applications and remaining limitations are well explained in the paper,' accepting these constraints.

Both evaluations address performance variation across cell lines (C137). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, noting it as an honest assessment of observed variations. Peer Reviewer 3 also supports this limitation, noting the classifier 'is not yet at a point where it can be reliably applied to functional genomics assays' with diverse nuclear aberrations.

Both evaluations address speculation about nuclear atypia's role (C140-C141). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting the hypothesis is not directly tested and requires experimental validation. Peer reviewers support this interpretation without challenge, accepting it as a reasonable explanation for observed differences.

OpenEval supports claims about Mps1i treatment effects on RPE1 cells (C34, C37-C42) with detailed figure references showing MN frequency increases and chromosome content. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific experimental details.

OpenEval supports proximity-based MN-nucleus assignment accuracy (C49-C52) with specific metrics (97% accuracy, 3.3-fold distance difference). No corresponding peer review evaluation found for this technical validation detail.

OpenEval supports the observation that VCS MN performs poorly on higher resolution confocal images (C71), which motivated MNFinder development. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for this specific technical limitation.

Both address overall capabilities of developed methods (C122-C124, C138). OpenEval supports these summary statements based on comprehensive performance data. Peer reviewers affirm the tools as 'powerful' and 'rigorous,' though this evaluation also includes C123 which overlaps with VCS MN performance.

Partial overlap on summary capabilities (C122). OpenEval supports overall method capabilities. Peer reviewers' R2 focuses on MNFinder specifically, affirming it as filling a gap in the field with rigorous benchmarking.

OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN the claims about RPE1 cells with reduced cGAS expression and predictions for other cell lines (C142-C144), noting this is speculative and requires experimental validation. No corresponding peer review evaluation found addressing this specific limitation.

Both address future applications of visual cell sorting (C145-C151). OpenEval supports these as reasonable extensions with appropriate citations. Peer reviewers affirm the potential impact, with partial overlap on C145, emphasizing the method could 'change the way we isolate and study MN-containing cells.'

OpenEval supports extensive background claims about MN biology and prior methods (C1-C4, C9-C27, C32-C33, C35-C36, C46, C62) as well-supported by literature citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these background/context claims.

OpenEval supports the documented limitation of Deep Retina segmenter for nucleus detection (C47) with quantified solidity measurements. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for this specific technical detail.
